title: ALPACA: Anonymous Blocklisting with Constant-Sized Updatable Proofs
abstract: In recent years, online anonymity has become increasingly important but is under threat due to the challenges of moderating anonymous spaces. A promising cryptographic solution, known as anonymous blocklisting, allows users to post anonymously while still enabling moderation. Moderation via anonymous blocklisting roughly works by requiring that when users post a message they attach a cryptographic proof that they did not author any posts on a "blocklist". Existing anonymous blocklisting schemes are unfortunately still far from achieving practical performance for large blocklists. This is essentially due to all prior works requiring a user to (cryptographically) reprocess blocklist entries many times. Relatedly, prior works have relatively high verification times and proof sizes. In this work, we introduce ALPACA, the first anonymous blocklisting system with the property that a user only needs to do a constant amount of work per blocklist entry. Thus, our scheme has asymptotically optimal performance. Our scheme is also the first to have verification times and proof sizes that are independent of the number of blocklist entries. Our key technique is a new variant of incrementally verifiable computation (IVC), designed to ensure anonymity. Along the way, we introduce new definitions to formally establish security. On a mid-range laptop, ALPACA's proof generation time is always 6.15 seconds and proof size is 25.6KBs. On a server, the verification time is always 400ms.

Moderation via anonymous blocklisting roughly works by requiring that when users post a message they attach a cryptographic proof that they did not author any posts on a “blocklist”. Existing anonymous blocklisting schemes are unfortunately still far from achieving practical performance for large block- lists. This is essentially due to all prior works requiring a user to (cryptographically) reprocess blocklist entries many times. Relatedly, prior works have relatively high verification times and proof sizes. In this work, we introduce ALPACA, the first anonymous blocklisting system with the property that a user only needs to do a constant amount of work per blocklist entry. Thus, our scheme has asymptotically optimal performance. Our scheme is also the first to have verification times and proof sizes that are independent of the number of blocklist entries. Our key technique is a new variant of incrementally verifiable computation (IVC), designed to ensure anonymity. Along the way, we introduce new definitions to formally establish security. On a mid-range laptop, ALPACA's proof generation time is always 6.15 seconds and proof size is 25.6KBs. On a server, the verification time is always 400ms. 1. Introduction Anonymous spaces, in which a user does not need to divulge their identity to participate, have historically been an extremely important part of how users interact with the Internet. From the earliest Usenet forums, which allowed anonymous posting via invalid emails [1], to 4chan and other anonymous message boards [2], and modern anonymous so- cial apps like YikY ak [3], users continue to seek out spaces where they can interact and discuss controversial topics without fear of censure or retribution. Anonymous browsing tools like TOR even allow users to interact anonymously with websites not designed to allow this [4]. Despite the importance of anonymous spaces on the inter- net, anonymity online is increasingly under threat [1, 5-7]. This is in large part because of the difficulty of moderat- ing anonymous spaces: the very freedom that anonymity provides can enable-or even magnify [8]-harassment, threats, and cyberbullying. This leads to external pressure on providers to shut down anonymous spaces: for example, the widely-used YikY ak app was banned on many college campuses and ultimately shut down in part because of the prevalence of cyberbullying; it was recently revived but is again facing bans [9, 10]. It also leads to providers choosing to add friction or ban anonymous interactions with services: for example, it is difficult to edit Wikipedia over TOR- most TOR exit nodes are IP-blocked from making edits to Wikipedia. This leads to exclusion of users from vulner- able populations who actually need the ability to interact anonymously [11] and deprives the wider community of their contributions: e.g., anonymous editors on Wikipedia actually make high-quality contributions [12]. The risks of non-anonymous interactions to vulnerable populations are all too real: the Syrian Wikipedia developer and dissident Bassel Khartabil was arrested and ultimately executed by the Syrian government in 2015, allegedly in part because of his online activism [13]. Cryptography can help resolve the seeming tension be- tween anonymity and moderation. A key technical tool for this is anonymous blocklisting (AB). In AB, users can post messages on a public bulletin board anonymously; however, the provider can add messages that violate policies to a “blocklist”. To post, users must prove that they are not the author of any of the messages on the blocklist. A long line of work, starting with the seminal BLAC paper [14], has built AB schemes based on zero-knowledge proofs with various different performance profiles; the more recent SNARK- Block work [15] was the first to apply modern zkSNARKs to anonymous blocklisting. However, previous works suffer from notable drawbacks: first, their proof sizes and verifying time are not scalable to large blocklists; even the state- of-the-art SNARKBlock has costs that are asymptotically superlinear in the total number of blocks. Second, they require even honest clients to re-do work for blocks already processed. In this work, we present ALPACA, the first anonymous blocklisting scheme with asymptotically constant online cost *&&&4ZNQPTJVNPO4FDVSJUZBOE1SJWBDZ 41 ¥ +JXPO,JN6OEFSMJDFOTFUP*&&& %0*41 and proof size. ALPACA also does not re-do any work; once a client processes a block, they never need to pro- cess it again. Our main contributions are (1) the ALPACA scheme itself, built as a new and nontrivial application of incrementally verifiable computation (IVC) [16], (2) a de- tailed provable-security analysis, including new game-based security definitions that may be of independent interest, and (3) a new variant of incremental verifiable computation that provides an iteration-hiding guarantee not given by prior schemes, and an extension of the Nova IVC scheme [17] that satisfies iteration-hiding. We also perform a detailed evaluation of ALPACA, which gives evidence for its prac- ticality: for example, updating the local non-membership proof of ALPACA is up to 35 × faster than SNARKBlock, the previous state-of-the-art. 1.1. Overview of Contributions ALPACA starts with representing the blocklist as an append- only list. As in prior work, each entry in the list in ALPACA contains a token for a posted message; to post, a user must prove none of the tokens are for their messages. The key conceptual idea of our construction is that lists are recursively-defined data structures. A list is either empty, or it comprises a head item and a tail, which is itself a list. Thus, ALPACA uses a naturally recursive proof primitive-incrementally verifiable computation (IVC)-to generate non-membership proofs in two steps: (1) the token in the head of the list is not the user's, and (2) the user knows a proof that none of the tokens in the tail of the list are theirs either. To post messages, the user proves, via a zkSNARK tailored to the IVC scheme, that they know a valid IVC proof of non-membership on the blocklist, and uses an auxiliary zkSNARK to prove well-formedness of the new message's token. This is roughly how the steady-state func- tionality of ALPACA works for enrolled users that are never blocked-see §5 for more details-but does not give us two important pieces of functionality a real blocklisting system needs. First, it needs to be possible to un-block users. Temporary blocks are extremely common in applications like Wikipedia, where blocks are an attempt at corrective action rather than punishments [18]. The second important piece of functionality is that we need to allow users to “cold-start” in the system without needing to process every historical entry on the blocklist, even ones from before they registered. ALPACA enables unblocking by having the provider pub- licly post a “ban-over” signature on an entry in the list. If a user was blocked from posting because of this entry, they can use this signature to skip the token check for that entry and continue to update their non-membership proof. We use a similar idea for cold-starting: when a user obtains their credential, the identity provider (blindly) signs it along with the current head of the list; this lets them skip the update step for everything before. We carefully adapt the basic design to allow for these extensions with sacrificing security. In §6, we prove our scheme is anonymous (i.e., proofs hide identities), block- listable (i.e., blocks cannot be bypassed), and non-frameable (i.e., users cannot be blocked for a message they did not post). To do this, we developed novel game-based definitions of security for these properties (§3.1). Our definitions are likely to be of independent interest for future research in anonymous blocklisting and related areas. One real-world issue our anonymity definition captures is cold-starting: that is, the fact that users may enter the system at different times. In trying for the first time to prove our scheme with this definition we made the observation that with standard IVC the scheme is not necessarily secure. This is because existing formulations of IVC requires the number of iterations of the function F to be revealed publicly in the proof [16, 17, 19-21]. This means that two users who join at different times can immediately be distinguished based on the number of blocks they have processed since starting. Fixing this issue requires designing a new IVC vari- ant with an iteration-hiding property. This is technically nontrivial because the iteration count is critically required by algorithms that show up in the knowledge soundness proofs for existing schemes. We resolve this by carefully embedding the iteration count inside the IVC proof in such a manner that it can be efficiently hidden before the proof is published but still accessible by procedures in the soundness proof. We believe this result is also of independent interest; it is plausible that other applications may require hiding the iteration count. ALPACA instantiates this high-level design with our iteration-hiding extension (§4) of the Nova IVC scheme [17]. Users locally maintain their non-membership proofs as Nova IVC proofs of repeated application of a carefully-designed function F to the blocklist. To post, users “wrap” the IVC proof, which is not zero-knowledge, in an outer zkSNARK, and produce an auxiliary zkSNARK that their credential produced the new message's token. Our local state size, online proving time, proof size, and verification time are all asymptotically constant-they do not depend at all on the size of the blocklist. However, getting practical performance required non-trivial design and engineering effort. We instantiate our function F with SNARK-friendly cryptographic primitives, such as the Po- seidon hash function [22] and the Schnorr signature scheme over the Pasta curve cycle [23]. This minimizes the R1CS constraint count of F , which is critical because it minimizes the time needed to update the non-membership proof. In section 7, we give our evaluation of ALPACA. Our function F for non-membership proof only requires 31842 R1CS constraints, and other statements proved during post- ing are only 16287 R1CS constraints. We also measured prover time, proof size, and verifier time taken as the block- list grows. We empirically verified performance is indepen- dent of blocklist size. We also found the ALPACA prover time is better than SNARKBlock after 220 blocks, verifier time is better after 217 blocks, and proof size is always better.
